newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian wool market jump enthuses trade.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian wool market jump enthuses trade.

text.p: A jump in Australian wool prices at auction and on the Sydney Futures Exchange enthused brokers on Thursday who see a return to better market fundamentals.
The eastern market indicator jumped by 28 cents to 612 cents a kg clean at auctions in Sydney and Geelong on Wednesday, one of the biggest gains seen for many months.
Greasy wool futures also put in a strong performance on Wednesday, with more than 100 lots changing hands against the normal volume of 10 to 15 a day.
"It was an excellent day in wool," said Gary Booth of Ord Minnett Jardine Fleming Futures.

Ted Harnett, general manager wool for pastoral house Wesfarmers Dalgety Ltd, said the main driving force in Wednesday's auction market was limited quantities for sale -- about 50,000 bales were slotted for sale this week -- although demand also picked up.
Wesfarmers Dalgety expected the market would gradually improve, with demand building up and supply and demand coming into balance, he said.
A low pass-in rate of about four percent on Wednesday was also pleasing, given the 25.0-30.0 percent pass-in rates of a year ago, he said.
Higher prices accompanied the rise in volume, with the April 1997 contract rising to 746 cents a kg clean from 731 cents on Tuesday.
Wednesday's price gains continued in SFE futures trading on Thursday, with the April contract rising further to 750 cents at midday (0100 GMT) before slipping back slightly.
Turnover, however, dropped back, to 24 lots traded at around midday.

Harnett pointed out, however, that the auction market rise was from a low base and that many producers were selling at less than their costs of production. Not so long ago the market was over 700 cents a kg, said.
Booth was much more enthusiastic about wool's rise.
Wednesday's strong futures performance was the result of many factors coming together, he said.
Several buyers had to meet shipment deadlines on Wednesday, Booth said. He declined to name names.
Wool International's forward selling of all of its legally allowable quantity for the March quarter had removed the stockpile overhang from the wool market, he said.

Other fundamentals combining to spur the market were the decline in Australia's wool stockpile to less than two million bales from almost five million bales in 1991, and a decline in the supply of wool, partly with a shift by growers into sheep for meat instead of wool.
The drop in the stockpile was a "great sign," he said. "Wool International has no wool to sell."
Mexico's decision to eliminate tariffs on wool tops, noils and waste gave Australia access to the entire North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) area, he said.
Falling interest rates and a declining Australian dollar also helped, he said.
Ords were seeing woolgrowers emerging to hedge as well as interest by buyers to purchase wool or hedge through the futures exchange, he said.
Enquiries were "excellent, very strong," he said.
-- Michael Byrnes Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
